newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ faces knife-edge election under new rules.
newsitem.headline: NZ faces knife-edge election under new rules.

text.p: A tax-cutting government which only last week was polling twice the support of its nearest rival is in danger of losing power in New Zealand's general election on Saturday.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger's conservative National Party, in power since 1990, has presided over the strongest economic growth in a generation and is promising further tax cuts next year on top of a first round last July.

Opponents, especially a resurgent Labour Party, say recovery has passed most ordinary people by. They say rises in student fees and hospital waiting lists bear witness to crises in education and health.

Opinion polls show Labour fast closing the gap on National, raising leader Helen Clark's chances of becoming New Zealand's first woman prime minister. A TV poll last week showed National on 40 percent to Labour's 18, but a weekend newspaper poll put the gap at 34-28.

But a switch to German-style proportional representation from British-style first-past-the-post system means neither National nor Labour could govern alone. Each would need allies as the country enters a new era of coalition politics.
National must pin its hopes on the morals-based Christian Coalition and radical free-market Act New Zealand, neither of which is assured of winning seats.

Labour's prospects are just as murky. It will need to reach a deal with the New Zealand First Party, which seeks curbs on foreign investment, or the left-wing Alliance, which wants heavy tax increases to fund free health and education.

Bolger calls the left-wing parties a "three-headed monster", saying they would roll back 12 years of reform which turned New Zealand from one of the Western world's most regulated and protected economies into one of the most open and competitive.

"The 1996 election is a referendum on whether we go forward or we go back," he said last week. "It is a referendum on whether we have low taxes or high taxes, whether we have low interest rates, or high interest rates, whether we have freedom in the workplace or return to union domination and whether we have investment in jobs or high unemployment."

But the doom-laden warnings appeared to backfire, as financial markets betrayed few election nerves and international credit rating agency Standard and Poor's said New Zealand's AA+ rating was not in jeopardy.

Opposition leaders said the prime minister was running scared, accusing him of treason and economic sabotage when he encouraged overseas investors to wait until after the election before committing themselves.

The trouble for Bolger is that economic growth, which peaked above six percent, has been twinned with high interest rates and a surging New Zealand dollar as the central bank has wrestled in vain to keep inflation in its 0-2 percent target band. Farmers, manufacturers and homeowners have all felt the pinch.

"This is the dilemma the government is in; if they bid up too strongly the economic recovery, voters immediately start asking: what have I seen of this recovery?" said Rod Alley, political scientist at Victoria University in Wellington.
"People are saying: 'if all this recovery's around, why are you scaring us so much about drastic results if we vote for anyone else?' "
